one_line: A selfie-style expert talking-head video with burned-in captions that explains why a big reaction to toddler hitting backfires and gives a four-step calm response (stay calm and okay the feeling, hold the boundary with words and action, teach coping skills later).

hook.visual: Woman in a white sweater filmed selfie-style in a living room, looking straight into the lens and speaking from frame 0. A dark rounded title bar sits at the top for the whole video, and a rounded caption with a small question-mark sticker sits at lower right.
hook.on_screen_text: Persistent title bar: "How to Put an End to Your Toddler's Hitting". Bottom caption 0-3s: "WANT TO KNOW THE SECRET TO GET YOUR TODDLER TO STOP HITTING?" (English on screen, no translation needed)
hook.first_spoken_line: Want to know the secret to getting your toddler to stop hitting? (English, Whisper)
hook.why_it_stops_the_scroll: Observed: the title bar and first caption name one specific, scary, common parent problem (toddler hitting) and promise a 'secret'. Observed in transcript: the answer is withheld behind a three-line list of what NOT to do (3.3-10.7s). Inferred: a parent who has just seen their toddler hit stays to learn the alternative.

beats.observed: Direct-to-camera selfie shot, living room background; title bar at top, question caption with a ? sticker at lower right.
beats.spoken: Want to know the secret to getting your toddler to stop hitting?
beats.on_screen_text: How to Put an End to Your Toddler's Hitting / WANT TO KNOW THE SECRET TO GET YOUR TODDLER TO STOP HITTING?

beats.observed: Black caption boxes stack one line at a time. At about 8-10s she raises a finger and opens her mouth wide, miming a scolding 'No!'.
beats.spoken: It's not threatening them. It's not shaming them. It's not coming in hot with a no. We do not do that.
beats.on_screen_text: It's not threatening them. / It's not shaming them. / It's not coming in hot with a, "No! We do not do that!"

beats.observed: Caption collapses to one block; she gestures with a raised hand and leans toward the camera.
beats.spoken: Because when you blow up, when you lose your cool, when you come in hot with a big no, two things happen.
beats.on_screen_text: Because when you blow up, when you lose your cool, when you come in hot with a big "NO," two things happen:

beats.observed: Large facial expressions and hand waves. A small white side-note box appears at upper right from roughly 19s to 28s.
beats.spoken: One, for a toddler, a big reaction can actually feel exciting and fun and it gives them that attention that they so desperately crave from us, which means we can accidentally reinforce that behavior to happen more.
beats.on_screen_text: 1) For a toddler, a BIG reaction can actually feel exciting and fun, and it gives them the attention they so desperately crave from us. / Which means we can accidentally reinforce that behavior to happen more. / Side note: "Even if the reaction/ attention is negative, it can still exacerbate the behavior."

beats.observed: She widens her eyes and waves a hand across the lens at about 32s. A second side-note box sits at upper right.
beats.spoken: Two, it can make your already emotionally volatile kid more volatile in the moment.
beats.on_screen_text: 2) It can make your already emotionally-volatile kid MORE volatile in the moment. / Side note: "It's like adding fuel to the already-chaotic fire!"

beats.observed: Caption block, speaker mostly steady with one open-palm gesture.
beats.spoken: When you go the other direction and you do nothing, your kid learns that hitting is totally okay.
beats.on_screen_text: When you go the other direction and you do nothing, your kid learns that hitting is totally okay.

beats.observed: Caption style switches to a bold sans-serif rounded pill for the pivot question at 44s, then back to serif boxes. She softens her expression and shows an open hand while saying 'okay the feelings'.
beats.spoken: So how do you stop the hitting? Come in calm, confident, I know that part's hard, and okay the feelings. It's okay to feel mad. The feeling that your child's feeling in the moment is okay. The behavior is not.
beats.on_screen_text: SO HOW DO YOU STOP THE HITTING? / Come in calm & confident (I know that part's hard), and okay the feelings. / The feeling that your child's feeling in the moment is okay. / The BEHAVIOR is not.

beats.observed: She holds up fingers while introducing the boundary, then looks down and to the side while reciting the script (1:04-1:06). No child or baby is visible in frame.
beats.spoken: So next you come in with a boundary and I'm talking words and action. Together, it sounds like this. It's okay to feel mad. It is not okay to hit. I'm picking up baby to keep him safe.
beats.on_screen_text: So next you come in with a boundary, and I'm talking words AND action. / Together, it sounds like this: / "It's okay to feel mad. It is not okay to hit. I'm picking up baby to keep him safe."

beats.observed: Raised index finger at 72s. A white side-note box appears at upper right from about 77s to 81s.
beats.spoken: And then later, once they're calm, which is when the brain can take in new information and learn new skills, go back and talk about what they were feeling and what they can do next time when they feel that way or they're in that situation instead of hitting.
beats.on_screen_text: And then later, once they're calm - which is when the brain can take in new information and learn new skills... / Go back and talk about what they were feeling and what they can do next time when they feel that way... / Or they're in that situation INSTEAD of hitting. / Side note: "Teach those coping skills! Deep breaths, "angry chalk," etc."

beats.observed: Closer, calmer delivery with a thumb-point gesture. Final frame is a sans-serif pill; no end card, no logo, no link on screen.
beats.spoken: We're not always going to get it right. The goal is progress, not perfection, but this is how we're going to raise resilient generation.
beats.on_screen_text: The goal is progress, not perfection. / BUT THIS IS HOW WE'RE GOING TO RAISE A RESILIENT GENERATION.

payoff: The actionable answer arrives in layers: the calm-and-okay-the-feeling frame at about 46-57s, a word-for-word boundary script at 63-68s, and the 'teach coping skills later' step at 68-82s. About 70% of the runtime passes before the script.
cta: None inside the video (no spoken or on-screen ask in the frames or transcript). The caption asks viewers to join the account's course, Winning the Toddler Stage (ages 1-6), via link in bio.
share_or_comment_trigger: Inferred: parents send it to a partner who 'comes in hot', and save the exact script line. saves and shares are not in meta.json. Comments are only 2,420 on 4.52M views (about 0.05%), so the engagement shows up as likes, not discussion.
why_it_worked: 4.52M views, 15.3x the account median of 295K. The title bar and first caption name the exact problem and stay on screen for the full 89s, so every frame restates the promise (observed).

The answer is withheld behind a negation list and a 'two things happen' list (3.3-29.7s), then a counter-case at 36-43s closes the 'just ignore it' exit before the real answer at 44s (observed in captions and transcript).

93.6K likes at a 2.07% like rate is a normal organic profile, and the video ends on a copyable script plus a 'progress, not perfection' reassurance (inferred: reassurance lowers parent guilt, which helps sharing).
paid_signal: no: like_rate_pct is 2.07, far above the 0.3 level that suggests paid reach, and no ad labels appear in the frames. The caption sells the account's own course, so a boost cannot be fully excluded, but nothing points to one.

solo_route.how: 1) Barter with a parenting expert (child psychologist, early-years educator or OT) for personalised books in exchange for one 60-90s selfie take on a single pain point, in their own words. 2) You supply the structure: question hook, three-line 'what not to do' list, 'two things happen', a counter-case that closes the 'just ignore it' exit, then one word-for-word script line. 3) Edit in CapCut: a persistent title bar for the full duration, serif black-box captions at the lower third, small white side-note boxes for one-line takeaways, and a sans-serif pill for the pivot question. 4) Optional last card: a LumeBook page where the child hero takes deep breaths, shown as a tool for the 'teach coping skills when calm' step, worded with the expert's approval.
solo_route.needs: A credentialed barter expert who agrees to appear and to review every claim. No child on camera. The LumeBook tie-in must avoid promising behavioural outcomes.

lumebook_version.concept: Expert-led 60s selfie on toddler hitting using the same shape (what not to do, why, one script). Step 4, teaching coping skills in a calm moment, is the natural bridge to a personalised LumeBook story starring the child, presented as a calm-moment tool and not as a cure.

No child or baby is visible: the line 'I'm picking up baby to keep him safe' is spoken and captioned only.
